title: Hungarian essay
sentences: HUNGARIAN ESSAY
I. THREE-QUARTER ESSAY
The lyrical poetry of Petőfi
Petőfi Sándor, the world-famous great Hungarian poet,
as a lyric poet too holds an outstanding place in this land flowing with milk and honey, which he so splendidly portrayed in his descriptive poems.
In Petőfi's lyrical poetry the most important thing is subjectivity; in Arany János, however, we rather see objectivity gaining the upper hand.
While in Petőfi the naive, folk-like tone stands out so beautifully, in Arany János the folk tone is pushed into the background,
and its place is taken by linguistic beauty, which can nevertheless also be found in Petőfi's wonderful poems.
In Petőfi's lyrical poems we find the following beauties, namely: 1. folk simplicity, 2. national patriotism,
3. tropes and figures, 4. a son's love for his mother, 5. love poetry, and so forth.
Petőfi always strove for subjectivity, and he achieved his goal to the greatest degree,
for his poems find their way into the heart of the simplest peasant just as surely as into the shining halls of palaces awash in light!...
In his poems we see the golden-eared, beautiful great Hungarian Plain celebrated in song,
which no one but he was able to portray so beautifully, as he himself writes in his wonderful poem, which begins thus:
"You are beautiful, Plain, at least to me you are beautiful..."
Nevertheless Petőfi was able to portray not only the Plain, but also the Tisza and the "good old innkeeper", by whom his own father is meant.
In another poem he brought simplicity into relief even more, when the shepherd rides such a donkey
that owing to its shortness the shepherd's feet reach all the way to the ground.
Suddenly he hears that the shepherd's baby is dying, and he hurries home at once so that he may still find it alive, but finds only a corpse.
In his despair what else could the shepherd do but strike the donkey a mighty blow upon the head with his stick.
How wonderfully we see simplicity here, do we not—as the shepherd in his despair strikes the donkey upon the head!!...
Petőfi also has poems in which he sets up a contrast, for example "I turned into the kitchen..."
in the poem of that title, when he writes that his burning pipe went out, while by contrast his sleeping heart burst into flame.
Whereas before his pipe burned, now his heart burns, which in turn had slept before.
Even in this we can already see the contrast.
This is Petőfi's lyrical poetry, which plays a great role among the poets of the whole world to the glory of this beautiful golden-eared nation!!.
Skurek Ferenc VI.
b.
o.
t.
II.
ONE-PART ESSAY
Petőfi and lyric poetry
It is New Year's Eve night, 1823!
Outside the snow is drifting down in tiny flakes.
But oh, what great joy swells the breast of the local butcher, to whom a child was born in Kiskőrös on Saint Sylvester's night.
A tiny little infant.
With its black eyes, which still carelessly stare at the damp beams of the poor room, it now glances at its mother and cannot take its gaze off her...
The mother bends over the child with loving intimacy and with the care characteristic of true mothers straightens the cradle's hard (?), but white pillows...
What does this mother suspect?
This mother does not yet suspect that in the tiny cradle the once great Petőfi Sándor is resting his innocent childish dreams...
Petőfi!
When I write this word, a thousand memories rise up in my excited mind!!...
Wonderful poems ring and resound, which we read so eagerly, with flushed faces, at home among our loving parents and at school,
where our greatly respected teacher so beautifully explain ed the hidden beauties of the poems.
And before our mind's eye, while we listened to the explanation, like a dream-vision there passed the sunlit Plain,
the little farmstead, the outlaw, the shepherd and the donkey.
But who could enumerate them all!...
In Petőfi's lyrical poetry the subjective, personal element most stirs our hearts, while in Arany the serious, objective tone prompts manly reflection.
Petőfi, our great poet, our pride, with a lute in one hand and a battle-sword in the other,
rest in peace beneath the hidden mound of the battlefield of Segesvár in your rotting grave...!
Goldfinger Rezső VI.
b.
o.
t.
